title: Grade 6 Science — Thu, Jun 26
description: Light, Shadows and Reflections — Day 4 of 5: Solar and lunar eclipses
subject: science

questions.question: A solar eclipse occurs when:
options: Earth comes between the Sun and Moon
The Moon comes between Earth and the Sun, blocking sunlight from reaching part of Earth
The Sun comes between Earth and Moon
The Moon stops shining
questions.explanation: Solar eclipse: Moon → between → Sun and Earth. The Moon's shadow falls on Earth. Occurs at NEW MOON (when Moon is on the Sun's side of Earth). Not every new moon causes an eclipse because the Moon's orbit is tilted ~5° relative to Earth's.

questions.question: A lunar eclipse occurs when:
options: The Moon comes between Earth and the Sun
Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon — Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
The Sun is covered by clouds
The Moon moves to the far side of Earth
questions.explanation: Lunar eclipse: Earth → between → Sun and Moon. Earth casts its shadow on the Moon. Occurs at FULL MOON. The Moon appears reddish-brown during a total lunar eclipse ('Blood Moon') due to Earth's atmosphere bending red light onto the Moon.

questions.question: Order: Sun – Moon – Earth. This arrangement describes:
options: Lunar eclipse
Solar eclipse — Moon is between Sun and Earth
No eclipse — wrong order
Tidal effects
questions.explanation: Sun–Moon–Earth = solar eclipse (Moon blocks sunlight reaching Earth). Sun–Earth–Moon = lunar eclipse (Earth's shadow on Moon).

questions.question: During a TOTAL solar eclipse, people in the umbra region see:
options: Partial darkness
Total darkness — all direct sunlight is blocked by the Moon; stars are visible during the day
The Moon glowing
Brighter than usual sunlight
questions.explanation: In the Moon's umbra (total shadow), the Moon completely covers the Sun's disc. Total darkness for a few minutes. The Sun's corona (outer atmosphere) becomes visible. Very rare at any specific location.

questions.question: In a partial solar eclipse, people in the penumbra see:
options: Total darkness
Only part of the Sun is covered by the Moon — partial darkening
No effect
The Moon glowing red
questions.explanation: Penumbra region = partial shadow. Here, the Moon covers only PART of the Sun → partial solar eclipse. The sky dims somewhat but total darkness doesn't occur.

questions.question: Why does the Moon appear reddish ('Blood Moon') during a total lunar eclipse?
options: The Moon catches fire
Earth's atmosphere bends (refracts) red wavelengths of sunlight around the edge of Earth, projecting them onto the Moon — blue light is scattered away
The Moon becomes very hot
It's an optical illusion
questions.explanation: During a total lunar eclipse, Earth's atmosphere acts as a lens, bending red light (longer wavelength, less scattered) onto the Moon. Blue light (shorter wavelength) scatters away. This is the same reason sunsets are red.

questions.question: Why don't solar eclipses happen every new moon?
options: The Moon is too small
The Moon's orbital plane is tilted about 5° from Earth's orbital plane — most new moons the Moon passes above or below the Sun's disc, not directly in front
The Sun is too far away
Solar eclipses happen every new moon
questions.explanation: If the Moon's orbit were exactly in Earth's orbital plane, we'd have solar and lunar eclipses every month. The 5° tilt means the Moon usually passes slightly above or below — eclipses occur only when the Moon is near the intersection of the two orbital planes.

questions.question: Why should you NEVER look at a solar eclipse with naked eyes?
options: It is bad luck
The Sun's UV and infrared radiation can permanently damage the retina (solar retinopathy) even when the Sun appears dim — the Moon blocks visible light but UV still passes
The Moon blocks all harmful radiation
It is just a superstition
questions.explanation: Solar retinopathy: intense UV/IR from the Sun burns retinal cells permanently. During a partial eclipse, the dimmed Sun tricks you into looking without squinting, but harmful radiation continues. Use certified eclipse glasses (ISO 12312-2) or a pinhole projector.

questions.question: A total solar eclipse lasts only a few minutes at any location. Why?
options: The Moon moves slowly
The Moon's umbra is very small (radius ~100 km) — the shadow sweeps across Earth's surface at ~1,700 km/h, so any location is in the umbra for only 1–7 minutes
The Sun is very fast
Clouds block the eclipse quickly
questions.explanation: The Moon's umbra is a narrow cone (~100–170 km diameter at Earth's surface). As Earth rotates and the Moon orbits, this shadow sweeps a path across Earth (the 'path of totality') at high speed — only 1–7 minutes of totality per location.

questions.question: An annular solar eclipse occurs when:
options: The Moon is very close to Earth
The Moon is at its farthest point from Earth (apogee) — appears smaller than the Sun — doesn't completely cover the Sun, leaving a 'ring of fire' visible
Earth is at its farthest from the Sun
The Sun is smaller than usual
questions.explanation: Moon's distance from Earth varies (elliptical orbit). At apogee (farthest), Moon appears ~14% smaller → can't cover the entire Sun → 'ring of fire' (annular) eclipse. At perigee (closest), Moon appears larger → total eclipse possible.

questions.question: During a TOTAL lunar eclipse, can you still see the Moon?
options: No — the Moon disappears completely
Yes — it turns reddish-brown ('Blood Moon'), visible with naked eye because Earth's atmosphere bends red light onto the Moon
Yes — it glows white
No — only a professional telescope can see it
questions.explanation: During a total lunar eclipse, the Moon enters Earth's umbra but doesn't disappear — it turns reddish. Atmospheric refraction of red light illuminates it faintly. This is visible to the naked eye worldwide (wherever the Moon is above the horizon).

questions.question: Solar vs lunar eclipse: which can be seen by more people at once?
options: Solar eclipse
Lunar eclipse — Earth's shadow is larger than the Moon; when Earth's shadow covers the Moon, it's visible from the entire night-side of Earth simultaneously
Both are seen by the same number
Depends on the year
questions.explanation: A solar eclipse's umbra covers only ~100–170 km of Earth's surface — only a narrow strip of people see totality. A lunar eclipse is visible from the entire night-side of Earth (half the planet) simultaneously. Lunar eclipses are much more commonly observed by individuals.

questions.question: The 'path of totality' refers to:
options: The full orbit of the Moon
The narrow band on Earth's surface along which the Moon's umbra sweeps during a total solar eclipse — people within this path see a total eclipse
The Moon's shadow on the Sun
Earth's orbit around the Sun
questions.explanation: Path of totality: the track of the Moon's umbra across Earth's surface during a total solar eclipse. Typically ~100–170 km wide and thousands of km long. Only within this path is a TOTAL eclipse visible — outside it, only a partial eclipse.

questions.question: Why is a total lunar eclipse visible for longer than a total solar eclipse?
options: The Moon moves faster during lunar eclipses
Earth's shadow (umbra) is much larger than the Moon — the Moon takes 1–2 hours to cross it; the Moon's shadow on Earth is only ~100 km wide and crosses quickly (~1,700 km/h)
The Sun is farther away
Gravity slows the Moon during lunar eclipses
questions.explanation: Earth's umbra at Moon's distance is about 3× larger than the Moon. Total lunar eclipse can last up to 107 minutes. Total solar eclipse lasts only 1–7 minutes because Moon's umbra is tiny on Earth's surface.

questions.question: Ancient people feared eclipses. With our scientific knowledge, we can predict eclipses centuries in advance because:
options: Eclipses are rare and random
The orbits of Earth and Moon follow precise, mathematical paths (gravitational mechanics) — allowing astronomers to calculate all future eclipse positions and timings with great accuracy
We use computers to guess
Eclipses follow a 7-year cycle always
questions.explanation: Newton's laws of gravitation and orbital mechanics allow precise calculations. The Saros cycle (18 years, 11 days) repeats eclipse patterns. NASA predicts eclipses millennia in advance. Ancient fear came from lack of this understanding.
